for all possible values of and .

In terms of the joint distribution table, it means no matter which cell we look at in the middle of the table, the value of is the product of the corresponding numbers in the bottom row and right most column:

Explanation (added) ✎

This is the Lecture 6 test , applied to the events and . The difference is the word all: there is one such equation for every cell of the table, and every one has to hold. One cell that fails is enough to say “not independent”, so that is how a “not independent” answer is written: name the cell and show the two numbers.

Scatter plots for population or sample:

Explanation (added) ✎

Correlation measures how close the cloud is to a straight line, not how steep the line is. A line with any positive slope has correlation 1. A U-shaped cloud can have correlation 0 and still have a strong pattern, because only detects a linear one. Correlation also does not say that one variable causes the other.

9Linear combinations of independent normal random variables

Linear Combinations of Independent Normal Random Variables

Rule

If and are independent normal random variables, then will be a normal random variable for any choice of the constants and as long as they are not both 0.

To work with the resulting normal random variable, we need to know its mean and standard deviation (or variance).

Explanation (added) ✎

This is a special fact about the normal: the shape survives. Adding other independent variables does not usually keep the shape. For example, two dice are each uniform, and their sum is a triangle. The earlier rules give only the mean and the variance; this rule gives the shape as well, which is what allows a -table calculation.

“Not both 0” is there because is the constant 0, which is not a normal random variable.

Textbook Devore §5.5, p. 240, Proposition: any linear combination of independent normal variables is normal, for any number of variables and with possibly different means and variances; “in particular” the difference. Definition of a linear combination, p. 238, (5.7). §5.5 is not in the course outline’s schedule.

10Example: Jack’s and Bob’s trout

Example

Two different types of trout live in a large lake.

Species A has a mean weight of 1.5 pounds with a standard deviation of 0.4 pounds.

Species B has a mean weight of 2.0 pounds with a standard deviation of 0.6 pounds.

The weights of each type of trout are normally distributed.

Jack calls and tells you he caught a fish of type A.

A few days later, Bob calls and tells you he caught a fish of type B.

If we view catching a fish as selecting a simple random sample of size 1 and the weight of one person’s fish has no bearing on the weight of the other person’s fish, what is the probability Jack’s fish weighs more than Bob’s fish?

Let measure the weight of a fish of type A ← gives the weight of Jack’s fish

and measure the weight of a fish of type B. ← give the weight of Bob’s fish.

Added ✎ · not from the board

Seven questions on this lecture, written for this page with new numbers, in the style of the “typical exam question” list above. Work each one on paper first, then open the answer. Tick the ones you got; the tally is remembered on this device.

0 of 7 ticked
  1. Exam-styleReview: section 1 · Independence

    Are X and Y independent? Justify the way the instructor expects.

    Y = 0Y = 1Y = 2total
    X = 00.100.200.100.40
    X = 10.300.200.100.60
    total0.400.400.201
    Show the worked answer

    Not independent. Name one cell and show the two numbers:

    p(0, 0) = 0.10, but pX(0) pY(0) = (0.40)(0.40) = 0.16.

    Independence needs p(x, y) = pX(x) pY(y) in every cell, so one failing cell is enough. (To show two variables are independent you would have to check all six cells.)

  2. Exam-styleReview: section 7 · Covariance

    For the same table, find E(XY), Cov(X, Y) and Corr(X, Y).

    Show the worked answer

    E(X) = 0(0.40) + 1(0.60) = 0.6. E(Y) = 0(0.40) + 1(0.40) + 2(0.20) = 0.8.

    E(XY): only cells with x and y both non-zero count: (1)(1)(0.20) + (1)(2)(0.10) = 0.4.

    Cov(X, Y) = E(XY) − E(X)E(Y) = 0.4 − (0.6)(0.8) = −0.08.

    V(X) = 0.6 − 0.6² = 0.24. E(Y²) = 0.40 + 4(0.20) = 1.2, so V(Y) = 1.2 − 0.8² = 0.56.

    Corr(X, Y) = −0.08√0.24 · √0.56 ≈ −0.080.3666 ≈ −0.218.

    A weak negative linear relationship: when X = 1, Y tends to be a little smaller.

  3. Exam-styleReview: section 6 · What changes

    The instructor keeps coming back to this type. X and Y are independent with E(X) = 10, SD(X) = 3, E(Y) = 4, SD(Y) = 4.

    Find the mean and standard deviation of a) X − Y and b) 2X + 3Y.

    Show the worked answer

    a) E(X − Y) = 10 − 4 = 6.

    V(X − Y) = V(X) + V(Y) = 9 + 16 = 25, so SD(X − Y) = 5.

    Variances add even for a difference, and standard deviations never add directly: the answer is not 3 − 4 and not 3 + 4.

    b) E(2X + 3Y) = 2(10) + 3(4) = 32.

    V(2X + 3Y) = 2²(9) + 3²(16) = 36 + 144 = 180, so SD = √180 ≈ 13.42.

  4. Exam-styleReview: section 10 · Trout

    Machine A fills bottles with a volume that is normal with mean 12.0 oz and standard deviation 0.3 oz. Machine B: normal, mean 12.5 oz, standard deviation 0.4 oz. The machines are independent. One bottle is taken from each. What is the probability the bottle from A holds more?

    Show the worked answer

    Let X be A’s volume and Y be B’s. We want P(X > Y) = P(X − Y > 0).

    W = X − Y is a linear combination of independent normals, so it is normal.

    E(W) = 12.0 − 12.5 = −0.5. V(W) = 0.3² + 0.4² = 0.25, so SD(W) = 0.5.

    Standardize: z = (0 − (−0.5))/0.5 = 1.00.

    P(W > 0) = P(Z > 1.00) = 1 − 0.8413 = 0.1587.

  5. JustifyReview: section 7 · Covariance

    Show that Cov(X, Y) = E(XY) − E(X)E(Y), starting from the definition Cov(X, Y) = E((X − μX)(Y − μY)).

    Show the worked answer

    Expand the product: (X − μX)(Y − μY) = XY − μYX − μXY + μXμY.

    Take expected values term by term; the μ’s are constants:

    Cov(X, Y) = E(XY) − μYE(X) − μXE(Y) + μXμY

    = E(XY) − μXμY − μXμY + μXμY = E(XY) − E(X)E(Y).

    It is the same expansion as the variance shortcut in Lecture 8; with Y = X it becomes that shortcut, which is why Cov(X, X) = Var(X).

  6. ConceptReview: section 7 · Covariance

    a) If X and Y are independent, what is their covariance, and why?
    b) Is the reverse true? Test it with X equally likely to be −1, 0 or 1, and Y = X².

    Show the worked answer

    a) Independent gives E(XY) = E(X)E(Y), so Cov(X, Y) = 0.

    b) No. Here E(X) = 0 and XY = X³, which is also −1, 0 or 1 equally often, so E(XY) = 0. Then Cov = 0 − 0 · E(Y) = 0.

    But Y is completely determined by X, so they are certainly not independent. (Check a cell: P(X = 0 and Y = 1) = 0, but P(X = 0)P(Y = 1) = (1/3)(2/3).)

    Covariance and correlation only detect a linear relationship. This one is a parabola.

  7. ConceptReview: section 8 · Correlation

    Match each correlation to its description: −0.9, 0, 0.6.

    i) points scattered with no linear trend ii) points close to a line that slopes down iii) a loose cloud that slopes up

    Show the worked answer

    −0.9 ↔ ii) strong decreasing linear relationship.

    0 ↔ i) no linear trend.

    0.6 ↔ iii) moderate increasing linear relationship.

    The sign gives the direction and the size (always between −1 and 1) gives how tightly the points hug a line. Exactly ±1 means every point is on the line.
